description: We are first year aerospace undergrad students at the University of Bristol. We are a group of space enthusiasts tackling the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Our focus is on building a grounded, realistic mission concept where players must balance real-world engineering trade-offs—like fuel, payload limits, budget, and launch windows—to achieve their scientific goals. We’re turning authentic mission architecture into an engaging, strategic game.
summary: We have developped an educational interactive simulation game with different difficulty levels, tageted towards ages 7 to 12, 12 to 15 and 15 to 18. The game's objective is to design a space mission that satisfies the issue presented at the beginning. The game challenges the players to make decisions on the missions priorities, the design of the rocket ship, and the learn about the electronics needed. This game has the potential to encourage learning and curiosity of space missions.
details:
Design Concept and How it Works:
Our initial design concept is of an app which includes games that are specifically designed for age groups: 7-12, 12-15, 15-18. We are thinking of creating separate games for each of these age groups that will combine their respective school subjects and link it to space science, therefore enabling how to space science in a way that runs parallel to school. The current game design that we have developed is solely for the students of age- group of 7-12. We divided the game into different sections called mini- games where each mini- game would deal with each component of the rocket- building process which we have divided as aerodynamics, avionics and launch phase. The aerodynamics mini- game consists of an activity centred around building and designing a rocket. We wanted to create something that would be close to open rocket but without the excess of options and terminology that could confuse a kid. So we settled on a simple animated rocket that will show the different types of rocket parts and how to switch them around and play with it. The user can use the activity to play around and find out how to best choose components in order to have a successful launch. This activity will allow the user to understand how each component must be chosen with respect to the previous components chosen so it is not viable to small fins for a huge body. The second mini- game we developed is the avionics phase which will allow the users to unlock different avionics components upon completing each of the challenges. The challenges are structured in such a way that it will introduce the students to the flight computer, sensors and the power source. So the challenge for unlocking the flight computer is arranging the sequence of events that occurs when it comes across data. So, completing the challenge allows to user to understand how or by what process the data is read and processed and finishing this challenge allows them to unlock the flight computer. The challenge for unlocking the sensors is asking questions like what sensor is used for what. This will allow the student to understand what each sensor is used for. The challenge for unlocking the power source component is choosing the best option out of many. So what we have done is we have given three options (small, medium and large) and their respective energy capacity, weight an cost. The user is also given computer-calculated values for the max. allowable weight, cost and the energy capacity range for the particular spacecraft design that they chose. Now, the student has to choose a particular battery that is within the constraints mentioned below. Once the avionics phase is completed the game moves onto the launch phase where we just launch the rocket that we build. Once the rocket launches, it either shows mission succesful or mission fail. If its mission successful, it also shows the height reached and points accumulated. If its mission failed, it shows us the reason as to why it failed.
Benefits:
The game that we have designed as of now is only for the 7-12 year olds. so we realised that an integrated textbook is not going to be appreciated among the users and would feel a lot like schoolwork. We chose each mini- game with careful consideration on what it would mean for the young users.
The aerodynamics phase will teach the users on why it's important to play around until we get a viable option. This activity also allows the user to understand how each component must be chosen with respect to the previous components that were chosen so for example: it is not practical to have small fins for a huge body.
The various challenges present in the avionics phase helps the users to understand what the purpose for each component is without making it feel like a textbook. Also throughout the entire game we have displayed on top the max. allowable weight and budget for the entire rocket, so as the users add or change around the parts, the changes will also be reflected in the current weight and budget columns thus allowing the users to choose different components based on whether it is feasible or not with regards to this particular mission. This is a fun way to introduce the concepts of constraints to users and allows them to find and explore different options to stay within the constraints. This is a really good skill to foster in young children as the real- world aerospace sector also comprises of different factors to consider like budget, sustainability etc and allows to them to understand the various engineering trade- offs involved in the sector.
Intended Impact:
In an era where gaming is increasingly seen as trendy, we believe that the right kind of games can instill in children a sense of curiosity and the ability to troubleshoot when faced with challenges. This game can be used in a single- player, multiplayer and classroom setting. The classroom setting is something that we believe will develop a sense of camaraderie, healthy competition and scientific curiosity among peers while also enabling teachers to introduce the children to the world of science in the form of a fun and light activity. The classroom setting is basically allows two or more teams of multiple students to participate in the class as like an activity. We came up with this concept because we realised that most elementary school teachers find it difficult to introduce science concepts because they find it difficult to gauge how much is too much to teach and how to break the science behind it to elemnetary level while also making sure the child is engaged. We took up this concept because it does not include any of thes tresses involved in learning from a textbook but also subconsciously teaches the students the why behind rocket science without the risk of lack of engagement.

Jupyter Notebook (Python): used for coding
Claude (SI): used for developing the graphical user interface
itch.io: used for uploading the game in order to generate a publicly accessible link
NASA resources given in the page

We used an app called Procreate to graphically design the full design of the game and the logo of the app and the background and everything and tried to make everything as animated as possible to hold interest amongst the users.
